title: On Energy Stocks As A Portfolio Diversifier
gist: Gavekal argues energy has been the best-performing sector in both the S&P 500 and MSCI World over the past five years and is, with financials, one of only two sectors at all-time highs — and that because energy rallied during the 2022 Ukraine shock and the March 2026 US/Israel bombing of Iran while OECD government bonds fell, energy equities have displaced sovereign bonds as the better 'antifragile' portfolio buffer in an inflationary world. Note: this record is a paywalled teaser (~140 words), so only the opening argument is available.

insights.claim: Energy has been the best-performing sector in both the S&P 500 and the MSCI World over the past five years, a run that spans the post-2021 period rather than a single commodity spike.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Challenges the default assumption that mega-cap tech has owned the last half-decade of equity returns; a five-year lookback favouring energy argues for a structurally higher strategic weight than most benchmark-hugging portfolios carry.

insights.claim: Energy and financials are the only two equity sectors currently making new all-time highs, meaning breadth of new highs is concentrated in the two most inflation- and rate-levered parts of the market.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: A screen for sectors at new highs points to energy and financials as the momentum leadership to overweight, and implies other sectors (including tech-adjacent leadership) are trading below prior peaks.

insights.claim: Energy stocks outperformed precisely when the rest of the equity market struggled — in early 2022 at the start of the Russia-Ukraine war, and again in March 2026 when the US and Israel began bombing Iran.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: The pattern makes energy a geopolitical-shock convexity trade: hold it as crisis insurance that, unlike options, carries positive expected return in calm periods too.

insights.claim: OECD government bonds fell during the same turbulence episodes in which energy stocks rose, breaking the negative stock-bond correlation that underpins the standard 60/40 construction.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: If sovereign duration no longer rallies in risk-off, the hedging sleeve of a balanced portfolio needs replacing; swapping some govvies for energy equity is the concrete trade implied.

insights.claim: In an inflationary regime, the correct portfolio diversifier is an asset whose cash flows rise with the shock itself — which is why energy equities, not sovereign bonds, are the better 'antifragile' buffer.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: A regime-dependent rule for choosing hedges: in deflationary regimes buy duration, in inflationary regimes buy real-asset cash flows — use it to re-specify the hedging sleeve rather than just trimming bond duration.
insights.quote: in our new inflationary world, energy stocks are now a better “antifragile” portfolio buffer than government bonds

insights.claim: Gavekal explicitly frames the current macro backdrop as a 'new inflationary world', treating the inflationary regime shift as settled premise rather than open question.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: The asserted regime is the load-bearing assumption behind the whole energy-over-bonds call; if inflation re-anchors lower, the diversification argument weakens and duration reclaims the hedge role.
